rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians give the bāʾ names such as attachment, instrumental aid, and addition; each describes a real use.
rows.anchor: اختلفت عبارة النحويين في تسمية هذه الباء الجارة، فسموها مرة: حرف إلصاق، ومرة: حرف استعانة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attachment means joining one's sphere of capacity to the person or thing expressed after bāʾ.
rows.anchor: أما الإلصاق: فنحو قولك: تمسكت بزيد، وذلك أنك ألصقت محل قدرتك به،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Instrumental bāʾ marks a tool used to perform an action, as in striking with a sword or writing with a pen.
rows.anchor: وأما الاستعانة: فقولك: ضربت بالسيف، وكتبت بالقلم، وبريت بالمدية، أي: استعنت بهذه الأدوات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Additive bāʾ associates the act of passing with the person passed, as in passing by Zayd.
rows.anchor: وأما الإضافة: فقولك: مررت بزيد، أضفت مرورك إلى زيد بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians call bāʾ, kāf, and lām surplus because their one-letter forms are short and can blend with the following word.
rows.anchor: وأما قول النحويين (¬5): (الباء والكاف واللام الزوائد) فإنما قالوا فيهن:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expert grammarians avoid calling them surplus: bāʾ and lām are additive particles, while kāf is a preposition.
rows.anchor: وحذاق النحويين لا يسمونها زوائد، بل يقولون في الباء واللام: إنهما حرفا إضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These are functioning particles that govern the genitive case of the nouns they precede, like min, ʿan, and fī.
rows.anchor: وهذه حروف أدوات عاملة (¬5)، تجر ما تدخل عليه من الأسماء نحو: من وعن وفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prepositions supply a link because verbs such as wonder, pass, and go are too weak in ordinary usage to reach these nouns directly.
rows.anchor: وإنما جرت (¬1) الأسماء من قبل أن الأفعال التي قبلها ضعفت عن وصولها وإفضائها إلى الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added preposition makes those verbs reach their nouns; genitive distinguishes indirect connection from direct verbal accusative, while nominative is already occupied by the subject.
rows.anchor: فلما قصرت هذه الأفعال عن الوصول إلى الأسماء رفدت بحرف الإضافة، فجعلت موصلة (¬4) لها إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prepositional phrase remains in an accusative syntactic position, as shown when a following conjunct is accusative and by Sibawayh's cited verse.
rows.anchor: الجار والمجرور جميعا في موضع نصب (¬3)، ألا ترى أنهم عطفوا عليه بالنصب (¬4)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although bāʾ puts Zayd in the genitive, the phrase occupies the accusative position of a direct object, as Sibawayh's paraphrase and the accusative adjective show.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه: (إنك إذا قلت: مررت بزيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standalone particles at the beginnings of words normally take fatḥa; bāʾ in bi-Zayd is kasra because it resembles genitive lām.
rows.anchor: (وجميع (¬6) الحروف المفردة التي تقع في أوائل الكلم حكمها الفتح أبدا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bāʾ resembles lām because both are particles and both govern genitive nouns; the author defers the reason for lām's kasra to verse 2.
rows.anchor: فأما (الباء) في (بزيد) فإنما كسرت لمضارعتها (اللام) الجارة (¬7) في قولك: (المال لزيد)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb governed by bāʾ in the basmala is omitted because context supplies the sense: I began, or begin, in God's name.
rows.anchor: فأما المتعلق به (الباء) في قوله {بسم الله} فإنه محذوف، ويستغنى عن إظهارها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The written alif is dropped from bism Allāh because the familiar phrase is unmistakable and Arabic favors brevity when meaning is clear; unlike the less frequent formula in al-Wāqiʿa, al-Ḥāqqa.
rows.anchor: وحذفت الألف من بسم الله؛ لأنها وقعت (¬3) في موضع معروف، لا يجهل القارئ معناها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif remains when ism is attached to something other than God or when a different preposition precedes it.
rows.anchor: ولا تحذف الألف إذا أضيف (الاسم) إلى غير (¬5) الله، ولا مع غير الباء من الحروف،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif is also absent in pronunciation because it is a connecting hamza, for which the preceding bāʾ suffices.
rows.anchor: هذا في سقوطها في الكتابة، وأما سقوطها # في اللفظ، فلأنها (¬1) للوصل، وقد استغنى عنها بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine mercy means God's willing good and blessing for its recipients and is an essential attribute; human mercy is tenderness and compassion.
rows.anchor: معنى الرحمة في صفة الله تعالى: إرادته الخير والنعمة بأهله، وهي صفة ذات،

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿAbbās explains pairing al-Raḥmān with al-Raḥīm by treating the first as Hebrew and the second as Arabic.
rows.anchor: سألت أبا العباس (¬6) لم جمع بين الرحمن والرحيم؟ فقال: لأن الرحمن عبراني فأتى معه الرحيم العربي،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection cites pre-Islamic poetry using al-Raḥmān to argue that Arabs knew the name before Islam.
rows.anchor: ألا ضربت تلك الفتاة (¬4) هجينها ... ألا قضب الرحمن ربي يمينها (¬5)

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿAbbās replies that most pre-Islamic Arabs did not know the name; Quraysh said they knew al-Raḥmān only as a man in al-Yamāma, and a few poets learned it from scriptural communities.
rows.anchor: فقال (¬6): إن جمهور العرب كانوا لا يعرفون "الرحمن" في الجاهلية،

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: His intended distinction is that al-Raḥmān circulated across Hebrew and Arabic speech, while al-Raḥīm was distinctively Arabic and so clarified the pairing.
rows.anchor: ومراد أبي العباس أن الرحمن يتكلم به بالعبرانية (¬7)، وتتكلم به العرب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead holds that al-Raḥmān is an Arabic name derived from mercy, supported by Arabic patterns such as laḥfān, nadmān, and ghaḍbān.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه مشتق من الرحمة، وأنه اسم عربي لوجود هذا البناء في كلامهم،

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth treats al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as two names both derived from mercy.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: {الرحمن الرحيم} اسمان، اشتقاقهما (¬3) من الرحمة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda treats the two words as divine attributes meaning possessor of mercy.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: هما صفتان لله تعالى، معناهما ذو الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question What is al-Raḥmān? in 25:60 asks about the attribute, not the person's identity, so it does not prove the name was unknown; it may also express irreverence.
rows.anchor: فهو سؤال عن الصفة، ولذلك قالوا: {وما الرحمن}، ولم يقولوا: ومن، والقوم جهلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars say al-Raḥmān is more emphatic than al-Raḥīm, like ʿallām compared with ʿalīm; they call the former mercy for this world and the latter mercy for the afterlife.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا في أن أي الاسمين من هذين أشد مبالغة، فقال قوم: الرحمن أشد مبالغة من الرحيم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening fragment questions what thanks mean for a giver acting to obtain pleasure and answer compassion; its antecedent lies outside this segment.
rows.anchor: فأي معنى لشكر (¬3) من يعطي لاجتلاب لذته، ويجيب (¬4) داعي رأفته.

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr suggests that God praises Himself at the start of Scripture to teach people praise and thanks, earning them greater reward through their recitation as a kindness to them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر: ويحتمل أن يكون هذا ثناء أثنى به على نفسه، علم عباده في أول كتابه

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: On this reading, an imperative is implicit: people are told to say al-ḥamdu lillāh, just as 39:3 implicitly means that the polytheists say they worship idols to bring them near God.
rows.anchor: فقال: {الحمد لله رب العالمين} أي قولوا: يا معشر الناس ما إذا قلتموه علت منزلتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anyone who praises God thereby exposes himself to God's favor and reward.
rows.anchor: ثم إذا قال القائل: {الحمد لله} فقد (¬9) أثنى على الله تعالى، فيكون

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Asked how the best-formula hadith counts as supplication, a scholar answers that praise itself suffices: a servant need not state requests after praising God, just as a creature may be won by praise.
rows.anchor: أن بعض العلماء، سئل عن تفسير الحديث المروي: "أفضل الدعاء سبحان الله، والحمد لله،

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Ḥamd is broader than shukr: thanks follow a prior favor and do not praise someone's inherent good qualities, whereas praise can precede a gift and commend qualities.
rows.anchor: وإنما اختير (الحمد) على الشكر للمبالغة والعموم، وذلك أن الشكر لا يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet's indirect reference to praise as glorification and exaltation supports the breadth of ḥamd.
rows.anchor: فترجم بالثناء (¬1) والتمجيد (¬2) عن الحمد، فدل هذا على عموم الحمد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb can derive from nurturing: al-Aṣmaʿī defines rabb al-ṣanīʿa as completing and improving a craft, and rabb al-skin as filling it with butter.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي: (رب فلان الصنيعة يربها ربا إذا أتمها وأصلحها)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry about fat ripening in a skin and good deeds increasing supports the sense of completing and improving.
rows.anchor: فإن كنت مني أو تريدين صحبتي (¬5) ... فكوني له كالسمن (¬6) ربت له الأدم (¬7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the nurturing sense, God raises creatures and nourishes them through His blessings.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى (¬4) على هذا أنه يربي الخلق ويغذوهم (¬5) بما ينعم عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb can also mean owner: a person who owns a thing, or stands above someone as a master.
rows.anchor: الثاني: أن يكون الرب بمعنى المالك، يقال: رب الشيء إذا ملكه، ورببت (¬7) فلانا،

rows.speaker: صفوان بن أمية
rows.claim: Ṣafwān ibn Umayya uses rabb for a superior or master, preferring a Qurashī master to a Hawāzin one.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول صفوان بن أمية (¬9): لأن يربني رجل من قريش أحب إلي من أن يربني رجل من هوازن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anyone who owns something is its rabb; Arabic usage calls a person owner of a house or estate and includes the Prophet's question about owning camels or sheep.
rows.anchor: يقال: هو رب الدار ورب الضيعة (¬2)، وقال النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - لرجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word rabb may mean master without literal ownership, as in 12:42 and al-Aʿshā's reference to the lord of Kindah; God is owner and master in truth.
rows.anchor: ثم (السيد) يسمى ربا وإن لم يكن مالكا على الحقيقة (¬6)، قال الله تعالى: {اذكرني عند ربك}

rows.speaker: some linguists
rows.claim: Some linguists derive the owner sense from nurturing: an owner raises and brings up what he owns, while a master is an owner.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل اللغة: المعنى الثاني راجع إلى الأول الذي هو بمعنى التربية

rows.speaker: theologians
rows.claim: Some theologians say rabb has eternally described God as an essential attribute and derive it as abiding, from rabb bi-al-makān, to remain in a place.
rows.anchor: فأما ما يذهب إليه المتكلمون أنه لم يزل ربا (¬2)، وأن هذا من صفة الذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the theologians' proposed root as unattested to linguists: rabb does not mean remain, though arrabba can mean remain and could support their derivation.
rows.anchor: وليس يصح رب (¬4) بمعنى: أقام (¬5)، وأرب بمعنى: أقام صحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam on the faʿil pattern, and its derivation has two reported explanations.
rows.anchor: هو جمع (عالم) على وزن (فاعل) (¬1)، كما قالوا: خاتم (¬2)، وطابع، ودانق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One derivation connects ʿālam with knowledge or signs: every creature is a sign pointing to its maker, and ordinary speech uses al-ʿālam to mean all created things.
rows.anchor: فمنهم من قال: اشتقاقه من (العلم) و (العلامة)، وذلك أن كل مخلوق دلالة وعلامة

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Qatāda understand the worlds as all creatures, supported by Pharaoh's question and Moses' reply in 26:23–24.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الحسن (¬6) ومجاهد وقتادة (¬7) في تفسير العالم: إنه جميع المخلوقات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's transmission, Ibn ʿAbbās says that when ʿālamīn derives from knowledge it means rational beings, namely jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية سعيد بن جبير: هم الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم والأزهري
rows.claim: Abū al-Haytham and al-Azharī choose the jinn-and-human interpretation, since 25:1 calls the Qur'an a warning to the worlds and Muḥammad warned those two groups.
rows.anchor: واختاره أبو الهيثم (¬2) والأزهري (¬3)، واحتجوا بقوله: {ليكون للعالمين نذيرا}

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل وأبو معاذ
rows.claim: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl and Abū Muʿādh say the worlds here are the children of Adam, citing 26:165.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسين بن الفضل وأبو معاذ (¬5) النحوي: هم بنو آدم

rows.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda define ʿālamīn as rational beings in four communities: angels, humans, jinn, and devils; beasts are not called a world.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء (¬7) وأبو عبيدة: هو عبارة عما يعقل، وهو أربع أمم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word can denote the people of a single era: God's favoring the Children of Israel above the worlds in 2:47 means their contemporaries.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكر الله تعالى {العالمين} وأراد به أهل عصر واحد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All rational-creature readings are compatible with the knowledge derivation; those who hold them say Moses answered Pharaoh with a clearer description to confound him, not with a lexical definition.
rows.anchor: إنه لم يشتغل بتفسير العالمين، وإنما أراد تعريفه على وجه أظهر من الأول

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq chooses the all-creatures derivation and equates Lord of the worlds with Lord of everything in 6:164.
rows.anchor: وأبو إسحاق (¬5) اختار الطريقة الأولى، وقال: معنى العالمين: كل ما خلق الله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mālik is the active participle of milk, ownership; the source lists several verbal nouns and inflections of the verb.
rows.anchor: المالك في اللغة: (الفاعل) من الملك، يقال: ملك فلان الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The roots for ownership and kingship return to binding and fastening: a possessor binds a thing to himself, while a ruler binds and controls a people.
rows.anchor: وأصل الملك والملك راجع إلى معنى واحد، وهو الربط والشد، فمالك الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root appears in kneading dough tight, and in poetry where malik means to fasten or tighten something with a thrust.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا يقال: ملكت العجين أي شددت عجنه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Matālakahu means someone could not restrain himself; similarly, the malāk of a matter is what holds it together, such as the heart for the body.
rows.anchor: ويقال: ما تمالك فلان أن فعل كذا، أي لم يستطع أن يضبط نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Mālik is a kunya for old age, which holds a person back from impulses as youth does not; malaka also describes marriage because it binds the marriage contract.
rows.anchor: وأبو مالك: كنية الكبر والسن، كني به لأنه يغلب الإنسان ويشده عما يريد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There are two readings, mālik and malik; advocates of malik say a person can own property without being king, but a king necessarily owns, and malik can stand alone more readily.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا الحرف قراءتان (مالك) و (ملك) (¬4). فمن قرأ (ملك) قال: الملك أشمل وأتم؛ لأنه قد

rows.speaker: محمد بن جرير
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Jarīr argues for the malik reading by treating Rabb al-ʿālamīn as already establishing ownership, so the next phrase supplies a further attribute.
rows.anchor: واحتج محمد بن جرير (¬8) لهذه القراءة فقال: إن الله نبه على أنه مالكهم

rows.speaker: محمد بن السري
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn al-Sarrī distinguishes a king as owner of much property who also governs others and controls their affairs; every king is an owner but not every owner a king.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن السري: الملك (¬2) الذي يملك الكثير من الأشياء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supporters of the malik reading cite God's descriptions as King in 59:23, King of people in 114:2, and the question To whom belongs the kingdom today? in 40:16.
rows.anchor: ويقوي هذه القراءة من التنزيل قوله {فتعالى الله الملك} (¬4)، وقوله {الملك القدوس}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most linguists, including Abū ʿUbayda, Abū Ḥātim, al-Aṣmaʿī, al-Akhfash, and Abū al-ʿAbbās, prefer mālik as broader and more inclusive.
rows.anchor: وأكثر أهل اللغة اختاروا (مالك) أبو عبيدة، وأبو حاتم (¬6)،

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: They argue mālik applies to birds, domestic and wild animals, and every thing, whereas malik is normally said of people.
rows.anchor: وقالوا: إنه أجمع وأوسع، لأنه يقال: مالك الطير والدواب والوحوش وكل شيء،

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: They add that an owner necessarily possesses, but a king may hold a title over Arabs or non-Arabs without owning what he rules; mālik also combines verbal action and noun sense.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون مالك الشيء إلا وهو يملكه، وقد يكون ملك الشيء وهو لا يملكه

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: They understand the verse as saying God alone owns judgment among His creatures on that day.
rows.anchor: ولأن معنى الآية أنه يملك الحكم يوم الدين بين خلقه دون غيره، فالوصف يكون مالكا

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿAbbās reads mālik yawm al-dīn as able to bring about the Day of Judgment, a sense he says requires mālik rather than malik.
rows.anchor: واحتج أبو العباس لهذه القراءة فقال: (مالك يوم الدين) معناه يملك إقامة يوم الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mālik reading is also supported by 82:19, where the affair belongs to God; the lām of possession expresses the same meaning.
rows.anchor: ومما يقوي هذه القراءة من التنزيل قوله {والأمر يومئذ لله} [الانفطار: 19]

rows.speaker: supporters of the mālik reading
rows.claim: They answer Ibn Jarīr that scripture often gives a general statement and then a specific one, as in 96:1–2 and 2:3–4.
rows.anchor: ما ذكرت لا يرجح قراءة ملك؛ لأن في التنزيل أشياء على هذه الصورة قد تقدمها العام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the mālik reading, the active participle is linked to the time expression, while its understood object is judgments: God alone judges on that day, unlike earthly governors and judges.
rows.anchor: فمن قرأ {مالك يوم الدين} فقد أضاف اسم الفاعل إلى الظرف وحذف المفعول من الكلام

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: On Abū al-ʿAbbās's interpretation, the phrase omits a genitive noun and substitutes its complement: mālik means able to bring the Day.
rows.anchor: وعلى ما ذكره أبو العباس، الآية تكون من باب حذف المضاف (¬1)، وإقامة المضاف إليه مقامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In both readings mālik/malik yawm al-dīn is genitive as an adjective of the preceding noun; adjectives follow their referent unless detached for praise or blame.
rows.anchor: وأما إعراب {مالك يوم الدين} فالجر في القراءتين (¬2). وهو صفة الاسم، مجرور

rows.speaker: الأخفش أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says the adjective is governed by its status as a modifier, not by a preceding expressed word, just as a subject is raised by the abstract notion of initiation.
rows.anchor: فزعم الأخفش أبو الحسن أن الوصف يجري على ما قبله، وليس معه لفظ يعمل فيه

rows.speaker: الضحاك وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatāda define dīn as requital: God repays people for their deeds, as in the Arabic expression dantu-hu and 40:17, 45:28.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {الدين} قال الضحاك (¬11) وقتادة: (الدين) الجزاء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic usage and the cited verse and proverb use dīn for being repaid in kind.
rows.anchor: تقول العرب: دنته بما فعل أي جازيته (¬2). ومنه قوله: {أإنا لمدينون}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, and Muqātil gloss mālik yawm al-dīn as judge of the Day of Reckoning; Abū ʿUbayd prefers this explanation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس، والسدي، ومقاتل (¬5)، في معنى قوله {مالك يوم الدين}: قاضي يوم الحساب

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayd chooses the gloss judge of the Day of Reckoning.
rows.anchor: واختار أبو عبيد هذا القول (¬1).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn can also mean reckoning or sound accounting, as in 9:36; the saying the prudent person reckons himself uses the same sense.
rows.anchor: ومن الدين بمعنى الحساب قوله: {ذلك الدين القيم} [التوبة: 36] أي: ذلك الحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day is singled out as God's possession to magnify and make its terror felt, just as 100:11 singles out God's knowledge of people on that day though He knows every day.
rows.anchor: وخص هذا اليوم بأنه مالكه، تعظيما لشأنه وتهويلا لأمره، كقوله: {إن ربهم بهم يومئذ لخبير (11)}

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl analyzes iyyā as a pronoun with kāf attached in genitive; Abū ʿUthmān is also said to hold this view.
rows.anchor: ذهب الخليل # إلى أن (إيا) اسم مضمر، مضاف إلى (الكاف) وهذا -أيضا- مذهب أبي عثمان

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abū al-Ḥasan treats iyyā itself as a pronoun whose ending changes with the number and person addressed; kāf merely marks address, as in dhālika.
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو بكر (¬2) عن أبي العباس (¬3) عن أبي الحسن (¬4) أنه اسم مفرد مضمر يتغير آخره

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: According to the transmitted account, Abū al-Ḥasan disallows combinations such as iyyā-ka with iyyā of Zayd or falsehood.
rows.anchor: لا يجيز أبو الحسن فيما يحكى عنه: (إياك وإيا زيد) و (إياي وإيا الباطل)

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh reports hearing an Arab say that after sixty a man should beware of himself and young women.
rows.anchor: وقال سيبويه: حدثني من لا أتهم عن الخليل أنه سمع أعرابيا يقول:

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysān attributes to some grammarians the view that the full form iyyāka is a noun; others take its final yāʾ, kāf, or hāʾ as the pronoun and iyyā as support.
rows.anchor: وحكى ابن كيسان عن بعض النحويين أنه قال: (إياك) بكمالها: اسم.

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says kāf is genitive by adding it to iyyā, which can also take the other attached pronouns.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (الكاف) في (إياك) في موضع جر بإضافة (¬3) (إيا) إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author accepts only Abū al-Ḥasan's account: a pronoun is already maximally definite and has no need for the specificity of annexation.
rows.anchor: وليس يصح من هذه الأقوال إلا قول أبي الحسن (¬5). أما قول الخليل:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the full-word analysis as weak: like anta, iyyā is the pronoun, while the kāf's vowel marks masculine or feminine address.
rows.anchor: فكما أن ما قبل التاء في (أنت) هو الاسم، والتاء حرف خطاب، كذلك (إيا) هو الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pronouns divide into independent, attached, and hidden forms; they may be nominative, accusative, or genitive, though genitive pronouns have no independent form.
rows.anchor: واعلم: أن الضمير ينقسم إلى ثلاثة أقسام (¬9): ظاهر منفصل، وظاهر # متصل، ومستكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hidden pronoun is understood in a verb such as sat or stood because a verb cannot stand without a subject.
rows.anchor: وأما المستكن فهو ما كان مستكنا في الفعل كقولك: قعد، وقام، فالضمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyā is built on sukūn because it resembles a particle; its final alif is original, like the alifs in lā, mā, ḥattā, and kallā.
rows.anchor: واعلم: أن (إيا) مبنية على السكون؛ لأن فيها شبه الحرف، فهي مثل

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq reportedly glosses iyyā-ka naʿbud as we worship Your reality and derives iyyā from āya, a sign.
rows.anchor: عن أبي إسحاق قال (¬2): سمعته يقول وقد سئل عن معنى قوله: {إياك نعبد}

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح
rows.claim: Abū al-Fatḥ rejects that derivation: pronouns are built forms, not derived words; since iyyā is a pronoun it should not be considered derived.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الفتح: وحكى لي حاك عن أبي إسحاق قال (¬2): سمعته

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Naẓm explains iyyā as exclusivity: iyyā-ka ḍarabtu directs the act specifically to you, which also explains its use in warnings such as beware the lion.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب "النظم" (¬8): معنى (إيا) الاختصاص، وقول القائل: (إياك ضربت)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship is obedience joined to submission and humility, a form of abasement due only to God; ʿabd reflects a servant's lowliness and a well-trodden road is muʿabbad.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {نعبد} معنى العبادة: الطاعة مع الخضوع والتذلل، وهو جنس

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr says iyyā-ka is repeated for emphasis, like repeating bayna in the phrase between Zayd and ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر: وإنما كرر (إياك) للتوكيد، كما تقول: بين زيد وبين عمرو خصومة

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: He also notes that each verb independently selects an object: if placed after the verbs the phrase would be naʿbuduka wa-nastaʿīnuka, and both take the fronted iyyā-ka.
rows.anchor: قال: ولأن كل واحد من الفعلين يطلب مفعولا على حدته،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers emphasis as the reason for repeating iyyā-ka, since Arabic can leave the shared object unspoken after the first coordinated verb.
rows.anchor: والقول هو الأول (¬3)؛ لأن العرب إذا جمعت فعلين واقعين اكتفت بوقوع أحدهما من وقوع الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object in 93:3, mā qalā, means mā qalāka and illustrates that coordination can share an object without repeating it.
rows.anchor: قال الله تعالى: {ما ودعك ربك وما قلى} [الضحى: 3] أراد (وما قلاك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Putting worship before asking for help does not establish chronological order: the conjunction wāw joins things without requiring sequence.
rows.anchor: والجواب: أن الواو عند النحويين لا توجب ترتيبا (¬6)، وإنما هي للجمع

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī says hadā-hu in religion means to guide him, while hadā-hu hidāya means to point someone to a road.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي: هداه في الدين يهديه هدى (¬2)، وهداه يهديه هداية، إذا دله على الطريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root meaning of guidance is indication; the leaders of horses and wild herds are called hawādī because they go in front to show the way.
rows.anchor: وأصل الهداية في اللغة: الدلالة. وهوادي الخيل والوحش التي تتقدم للدلالة (¬4).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term hādī broadened from a guide who leads by indication to any forerunner, including the leading animals, the neck, and a staff ahead of a traveler.
rows.anchor: هذا هو الأصل، ثم سمي كل متقدم هاديا وإن لم يتقدم للدلالة (¬1).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic examples from ʿUbayd, Ṭarafa, and al-Aʿshā use guidance for leading, limbs that lead movement, and a staff that either precedes or directs its bearer.
rows.anchor:
وقول طرفة:
للفتى عقل يعيش به ... حيث تهدي ساقه (¬4) قدمه (¬5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb hadā takes two objects and connects the second with ilā or lām, as illustrated in 37:23, 38:22, 7:43, and 10:35; awḥā behaves similarly in 16:68 and 99:5.
rows.anchor: والفعل من (الهدى) (¬4) يتعدى إلى مفعولين، ويتعدى إلى الثاني بأحد حرفي جر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition before the second object can be omitted, as in 1:6; ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ means guide us to it and make us follow it.
rows.anchor: وقد يحذف حرف الجر من المفعول الثاني في (الهدى) فيصل الفعل إليه بغير حرف جر (¬9).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Already guided believers still ask because a knower may encounter doubts that lead back to ignorance, so they request a subtle divine aid that preserves knowledge.
rows.anchor: قد تعرض للعارف شبه ينتقل بها إلى الجهل، فيحسن أن يسأل اللطيفة التي يتمسك معها بالمعرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They also do not know their future state, so they ask for confirmation in the truth they presently follow; guidance can mean steadfastness rather than rescue from error.
rows.anchor: لما كانوا لا يعلمون ما يكون منهم في المستأنف، حسن أن يسألوا الهداية على (¬2) وجه التثبيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's prayer that God guide ʿUmar is a wish for success and firmness, not a taunt that he is astray.
rows.anchor: وقد تستعمل الهداية لا من الضلالة كما قال الحطيئة لعمر رضي الله عنه:

rows.speaker: some of our companions
rows.claim: Some scholars say believers ask for future guidance because guidance is an accident that does not endure, so they ask God to create its likeness anew.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أصحابنا: يجوز أن يحمل على سؤال الهداية ابتداء فيما # يستقبل؛ لأن الهداية عرض لا يبقى،

rows.speaker: some scholars
rows.claim: Others treat the prayer as claiming the fulfillment of God's promise in 5:16 to guide those who follow His pleasure toward paths of peace.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: هذا سؤال، واستنجاز لما وعدوا به في قوله: {يهدي به الله من اتبع رضوانه سبل السلام}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣirāṭ has reported recitations with sīn, ṣād, zāy, and an intermediate ṣād-zāy pronunciation.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {الصراط} [الفاتحة: 6] (¬3)، فيه لغات قد قرئ بها: السين، والصاد،

rows.speaker: readers of sīn
rows.claim: The sīn readers derive the word from istirāṭ, swallowing, because the road swallows travelers; they say a ṣād before ṭāʾ would hide the root.
rows.anchor: فمن قرأ بالسين فإنه يقول: هو أصل الكلمة؛ لأنه من الاستراط بمعنى: الابتلاع (¬6)

rows.speaker: readers of ṣād
rows.claim: The ṣād readers say it is lighter and sounds better beside ṭāʾ because both are emphatic, unlike sīn, which is voiceless and farther from ṭāʾ.
rows.anchor: ويقول من يقرأ بالصاد: إنها أخف # على اللسان، لأن (الصاد) حرف مطبق ك (الطاء)

rows.speaker: readers of zāy
rows.claim: The zāy reading replaces sīn with a voiced sound, closer to ṭāʾ and light to articulate; they cite the Arab variant zaqr for ṣaqr.
rows.anchor: ويقول من قرأ بالزاي: أبدلت منها حرفا مجهورا (¬2) حتى يشبه (الطاء) في الجهر،

rows.speaker: readers of intermediate ṣād-zāy
rows.claim: Those who blend ṣād and zāy seek ease without making either pure sound and thereby confusing the word's root.
rows.anchor: ويقول من قرأ بالمضارعة (¬4): رمت الخفة، ولم أجعلها (زايا) خالصة، ولا (صادا) خالصة،

rows.speaker: ابن السراج
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sarrāj prefers ṣād for ease, euphony, and clarity; it is also the majority recitation, while pure zāy is unrecognized and should not control recitation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن السراج (¬6): الاختيار (الصاد) للخفة والحسن في السمع، وهو غير ملتبس،

rows.speaker: ابن السراج
rows.claim: He rejects the intermediate sound as a difficult, ad hoc articulation that is not an independent letter or a normal building block of words.
rows.anchor: وأما المضارعة (¬10) فهو تكلف حرف بين حرفين، وذلك أصعب على # اللسان؛ لأنه إنما استعمل

rows.speaker: صاحب الحجة
rows.claim: The author of al-Ḥujja argues ṣād is preferable because sīn before emphatic ṭāʾ creates an unwanted rise in articulation, as speakers already replace sīn with ṣād before qāf.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب "الحجة" (¬1): الحجة لمن قرأ بالصاد: أن (¬2) السين مضارعة

rows.speaker: صاحب الحجة
rows.claim: Replacing sīn with ṣād is even more apt before ṭāʾ than before qāf because ṣād is closer to ṭāʾ.
rows.anchor: فلأن يبدلوا منها (الصاد) مع (الطاء) # أجدر (¬1) من حيث كانت (الصاد) إلى (الطاء)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiqāma means straightness and continuation along one direction: qāma is to stand upright, aqāma to straighten, and qāwama to match in strength.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {المستقيم}: (الاستقامة) في اللغة: الاستواء، يقال: قام إذا استوى منتصبا،

rows.speaker: علي وابن مسعود
rows.claim: A report attributed to ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd from the Prophet identifies the straight path as God's Book; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: فروى علي وابن مسعود رضي الله عنهما عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه قال: "الصراط المستقيم: كتاب الله عز وجل"

rows.speaker: جابر ومقاتل
rows.claim: Jābir and Muqātil say the straight path is Islam.
rows.anchor: وقال جابر ومقاتل: (هو الإسلام)

rows.speaker: أبو العالية الرياحي
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya al-Riyāḥī says it is the way of the Messenger and the two who succeeded him, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي العالية الرياحي (¬2)، قال: هو طريق رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وصاحبيه

rows.speaker: بكر بن عبد الله المزني
rows.claim: In a dream report, Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī asks the Prophet about the straight path and is told it is his Sunna and that of the rightly guided caliphs; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وقال بكر بن عبد الله المزني (¬1): رأيت رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - في المنام

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The theologians of meaning say true religion is called the straight path because it reaches God's pleasure and lasting bliss, as a straight road reaches its destination.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: إنما وصف الدين الحق (¬3) بأنه الصراط المستقيم؛ لأنه يؤدي إلى الغرض المطلوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣirāṭ in ṣirāṭ alladhīna is an appositive restating the first ṣirāṭ in meaning, like calling one's father by the name Zayd.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {صراط الذين}: (صراط) بدل من (الصراط) # الأول (¬1)، وهو بدل الشيء من نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Relative pronouns such as alladhī and alladhīna are incomplete until their clause supplies a predicate, verb, circumstance, or conditional structure; that clause must contain a pronoun referring back.
rows.anchor: وقوله: {الذين} النحويون يسمون (الذي والتي) وتثنيتهما، وجمعهما: الأسماء الموصولة، والأسماء النواقص، والأسماء المبهمة، وذلك لأنها (¬4) أسماء لا تتم إلا بصلاتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alladhīna is indeclinable across nominative, accusative, and genitive because it remains incomplete without its relative clause and thus resembles a particle.
rows.anchor: و (الذين) لا يظهر فيه # الإعراب (¬1)، تقول (¬2) في الرفع والنصب والجر: (الذين)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A singular indeclinable relative gains case marking in the dual because particles are not dualized, but the plural is again a single form like hāʾulāʾ and remains indeclinable.
rows.anchor: قيل: إن جميع ما لا يعرب في الواحد مشبه بالحرف الذي جاء لمعنى، فإذا ثنيته بطل شبه الحرف

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq, following Sībawayh, al-Khalīl, and al-Akhfash, says the original form of alladhī was ladh on the faʿl pattern.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: وأصل (الذي)، (لذ) على وزن (عم)، كذلك قال سيبويه والخليل والأخفش

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح الموصلي
rows.claim: Abū al-Fatḥ al-Mawṣilī says the alif and lām in alladhī and related forms are fixed additions: other relatives such as man, mā, and ayy are definite without them, and the relative clause itself identifies alladhī.
rows.anchor: وأما الألف واللام فيه (¬2)، فقال أبو الفتح الموصلي (¬3): (الألف واللام) في (الذي) و (التي)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added lām is retained because alladhī enables a clause to describe a definite noun: ordinary clauses are indefinite, and the particle alif-lām cannot attach directly to a clause.
rows.anchor: قيل: إن (الذي) (¬1) إنما وقع في الكلام توصلا إلى وصف المعارف بالجمل، وذلك أن الجمل نكرات.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alladhī turns the sentence into a relative clause and marks the description as definite, as in the construction Zayd alladhī abūhu munṭaliq.
rows.anchor: فجاؤوا ب (الذي) متوصلين به إلى وصف المعارف بالجمل، وجعلوا (¬6) الجملة التي كانت صفة للنكرة صلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the verse, ṣirāṭ alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim means the road of those on whom You bestowed favor; the clause could describe an indefinite qawm directly, but not a definite group.
rows.anchor: وبيان ما ذكرنا (¬1) من الآية أن معنى قوله: {صراط الذين أنعمت عليهم} صراط القوم الذين أنعمت عليهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's inʿām is His favor and gift; niʿma is a verbal noun used in place of the infinitive inʿām, as nafaqa stands for infāq.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {أنعمت عليهم}، إنعام الله تعالى: منه (¬9) وعطاؤه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ in ʿalayhim may be pronounced with either kasra or ḍamma; kasra follows because yāʾ is related to kasra and the lighter transition is preferred.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {عليهم} يجوز كسر (الهاء) فيه وضمه (¬1). فمن كسر فلأن الياء أخت الكسرة

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh says wāw was added after masculine hāʾ just as alif was added after feminine hāʾ, balancing their added endings.
rows.anchor: زعم (¬5) سيبويه أن (¬6) (الواو) زيدت على (الهاء) في المذكر، كما زيدت (الألف)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says wāw was added to make the faint throat-produced hāʾ clearer with a labial long vowel; the connecting wāw drops in pause and changes to yāʾ after kasra.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: و (¬1) القول في هذه (الواو (¬2)) أنها زيدت لخفاء (الهاء)،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because hāʾ is a weak barrier, the preceding kasra acts as if it directly preceded the added wāw; that explains kasra in ʿalayhi and its retention in ʿalayhim.
rows.anchor: وبهذه (¬2) العلة كسرت الهاء في (عليه) وكان الأصل (عليهو) (¬3) فقلبت (¬4) الواو

rows.speaker: ابن السراج
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sarrāj explains the plural mīm's sukūn as lightening: the dual's alif already signals two, while the indispensable plural mīm lets speakers drop wāw without ambiguity.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن السراج (¬3): إنما أسكنوا لأنه قد أمن اللبس، إذ كانت (الألف) في التثنية قد دلت على الاثنين،

rows.speaker: ورش عن نافع
rows.claim: Warsh from Nāfiʿ pronounces plural mīm with ḍamma and links a following initial hamza with wāw; dropping hamza and moving its vowel requires the mīm to recover its original ḍamma and lengthen.
rows.anchor: وروى ورش (¬5) عن نافع (¬6) ضم الميم ووصلها بواو إذا (¬7) استقبلها # همزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warsh lengthens before an open hamza rather than transferring its fatḥa to mīm, which could make the plural resemble the dual; he follows the same pattern before other hamza vowels.
rows.anchor: فلما مدها عند الهمزة المفتوحة ولم ينقل حركتها إليها مخافة الالتباس فعل ذلك به

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī pronounce hāʾ and mīm with ḍamma at a following hamzat al-waṣl: mīm returns to its original vowel to break two sukūns, then hāʾ follows it.
rows.anchor: وكان حمزة والكسائي يضمان (¬7) (الهاء) و (الميم) عند ألف الوصل (¬8)

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr uses kasra for mīm as the usual vowel when breaking two sukūns and also gives hāʾ kasra to avoid a heavy kasra-to-ḍamma transition.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو عمرو (¬2) يكسرها عند ألف الوصل؛ لأنه يكسر الميم على أصل تحريك الساكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers who keep hāʾ kasra but give mīm ḍamma restore mīm to its original vowel without restoring hāʾ, which was not forced by the context.
rows.anchor: وأما من كسر (الهاء) وضم (الميم) عند ألف الوصل (¬4)، فإنه يقول: لما احتجت إلى حركة الميم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says those given favor were the people of Moses and Jesus before they changed God's blessings.
rows.anchor: فأما التفسير: فقال ابن عباس: {الذين أنعمت عليهم} [الفاتحة: 7]: هم قوم موسى وعيسى

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says God favored them by keeping them firm in faith and steadfast.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: أنعمت عليهم بالثبات على الإيمان والاستقامة (¬8).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies them with the people in 4:69 who obey God and the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هم الذين ذكرهم الله في قوله (¬1) سبحانه: {ومن يطع الله والرسول

rows.speaker: محمد بن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr says the verse is elliptical: guide us along the path of those You favored with guidance to the path, since Arabic omits words when context supplies them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جرير: في الآية اختصار، معناه: صراط الذين أنعمت عليهم بالهداية إلى الصراط.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayr can be genitive as an appositive to alladhīna or as its adjective; the adjective is valid because the relative phrase here is not a particular, singled-out group.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {غير المغضوب عليهم} (غير) (¬3) ينخفض على ضربين (¬4):

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayr may instead be accusative as a circumstantial expression or an exception meaning except those under wrath; as a circumstantial phrase it means not those under wrath.
rows.anchor: ويجوز (النصب) على ضربين: على الحال، والاستثناء (¬1)، أما الاستثناء:

rows.speaker: ابن السراج
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sarrāj additionally allows accusative as an implied aʿnī, I mean; al-Khalīl reportedly allowed it as a detached form of praise.
rows.anchor: قال ابن السراج (¬4): ويجوز عندي النصب على (¬5) (أعنى).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author chooses genitive: although ghayr and mithl are usually indefinite even when annexed to a definite word, a known thing with one known opposite makes ghayr definite.
rows.anchor: والاختيار الكسر (¬1). ولا يلزم وصف المعرفة بالنكرة؛ لأن حكم كل مضاف إلى معرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a known thing has one known opposite, ghayr annexed to that opposite is definite, as in movement versus stillness.
rows.anchor: فأما إذا كان شيء معرفة له ضد واحد، وأردت إثباته ونفي ضده، وعلم السامع (¬5) ذلك الضد

rows.speaker: صاحب الحجة
rows.claim: The author of al-Ḥujja says genitive ghayr is either apposition or adjective; apposition implies repeating the governing factor, as the repeated prepositions in 7:75 show.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب (¬7) "الحجة": أما الخفض في (¬8) (غير) فعلى البدل أو الصفة،

rows.speaker: صاحب الحجة
rows.claim: Apposition differs from an adjective because an indefinite can replace a definite and an expressed noun can replace a pronoun, neither of which is allowed for modifiers.
rows.anchor: وأيضا (¬3) فإن النكرة تبدل من المعرفة، والمظهر من المضمر (¬4)، وهذا مما لا يجوز في الصفة،

rows.speaker: صاحب الحجة
rows.claim: Apposition also repeats the understood governing case factor, while both apposition and adjective clarify the first noun.
rows.anchor: وكما أعيدت اللام الجارة في البدل (¬6)، فكذلك يكون العامل الناصب (¬7) والرافع في تقدير التكرير.

rows.speaker: صاحب الحجة
rows.claim: As apposition, ghayr has a clear meaning whether construed definite or indefinite, since both definite and indefinite apposition are accepted.
rows.anchor: فمن جعل (¬1) (غير) في الآية (¬2) بدلا، كان تأويله بينا،

rows.speaker: صاحب الحجة
rows.claim: As an adjective, ghayr can modify alladhīna here only because the relative phrase does not single out a particular group, making it like an indefinite description.
rows.anchor: وأما من قدر (غير) صفة و (الذين (¬7) فإنما جاز أن يصف (الذين) ب (غير)

rows.speaker: صاحب الحجة
rows.claim: A parallel is the definite al-rajul described by mithluka: the article does not identify a particular man, so the description remains nonspecific.
rows.anchor: قولهم: قد أمر (¬2) بالرجل مثلك فيكرمني (¬3)، فوصف الرجل بمثلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the verse, ghayr al-maghḍūb describes the favored people and is definite because one favored with faith is not under wrath.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قوله: {أنعمت عليهم غير المغضوب عليهم} فغير المغضوب عليهم، هم الذين أنعم عليهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 4:95, ghayr can modify the believers sitting out: the intended contrast is healthy nonparticipants versus those who strive.
rows.anchor: ومما (¬5) جاء (غير) فيه صفة (¬6) قوله: {لا يستوي القاعدون من المؤمنين غير أولي الضرر}

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ rejects accusative ghayr as an exception, arguing that a positive exception cannot be followed by negative lā in coordination.
rows.anchor: وأما من نصب (غير) على الاستثناء، فإن الفراء ينكر جواز (¬10) ذلك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those allowing exception say an exception resembles negation, so all came except Zayd can mean all came, not Zayd; lā can coordinate by meaning or be an addition.
rows.anchor: ومن أجاز (¬4) الاستثناء فإنه يقول: لا يمتنع دخول (لا) (¬5) بعد الحرف العاطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author concludes al-Farrāʾ's objection has no force, since lā can follow exception under either of those analyses.
rows.anchor: وإذا جاز دخول (لا) (¬1) مع الاستثناء لهذين الوجهين (¬2) فلا وجه لقول من أنكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā may also be added after ghayr as a circumstantial expression, adjective, or appositive; the Qur'an uses it in 57:29.
rows.anchor: وكذلك (¬4) يجوز زيادة (لا) في قول من جعل (غير) حالا أو صفة أو بدلا.

rows.speaker: some grammarians
rows.claim: Some allow added lā only after a preceding negation, but the author rejects that restriction and cites Saʿida al-Hudhalī's affirmative example.
rows.anchor: والذين يجوزون زيادة (لا) يقولون: إنما تجوز إذا تقدمه نفي (¬6)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before an indefinite, lā may be extra; if not extra, it either joins the noun as one genitive compound or contributes negation without affecting the noun's case.
rows.anchor: وهذا الحرف (¬6) -أعني: (لا) - يدخل (¬7) في النكرة على وجهين:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Examples of the compound include min lā shayʾ and bi-lā māl; lā plus noun functions as a single expression, like fifteen.
rows.anchor: وذلك نحو قولهم: (غضب من لا شيء، وجئت بلا مال) ف (لا) مع الاسم المنكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The non-compounding negator leaves case untouched, as in al-Nābigha's no uncle and al-Shammākh's sleepless night.
rows.anchor: والآخر: ألا تعمل (¬4) (لا) في اللفظ، ويراد بها معنى النفي،

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Naẓm says lā in wa-lā al-ḍāllīn prevents misreading al-ḍāllīn as coordinated with those favored; it marks coordination with ghayr, which implies negation.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب "النظم" (¬2): دخلت (لا) في قوله: {ولا الضالين} لمعنى من المعاني،

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: He illustrates the disambiguating role with a poem: lā before ʿUmar keeps him inside the Prophet's disapproval clause instead of starting a new sentence praising Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: أدخل (لا) (¬6) في قوله: (ولا عمر)؛ لأنه لو لم يدخل لاحتمل أن يكون انقطاع القصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root of ḍalāl is disappearance: water disappears into milk, and a disbeliever disappears from the path of truth; 32:10 uses the word for bodies lost in earth after death.
rows.anchor: وقوله: {ولا الضالين} أصل الضلال في اللغة الغيبوبة، يقال: ضل الماء في اللبن إذا غاب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḍalla can mean to hide or bury something, as in al-Mukhabbal's poem about Banū Qays losing their leader.
rows.anchor: ويقال: أضللت الشيء إذا غيبته، [وأضللت الميت إذا غيبته] (¬6) في التراب ودفنته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thus the astray person is absent from truth and has deviated from right guidance; the verb has reported variant forms.
rows.anchor: فالضال هو الغائب عن الحق الزائغ عن الرشد، ويقال: ضل يضل، وضل يضل لغتان،

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
rows.claim: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, attributed to the Prophet, identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: فأما التفسير فروى عدي بن حاتم (¬3) عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - في تفسير

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A second report says the Prophet at Wādī al-Qurā was asked by a man from Bali about two groups; he pointed to Jews as those under wrath and Christians as astray; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وروي أن رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - كان بوادي القرى (¬5) على فرسه (¬6)،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن مسعود ومجاهد وغيرهم
rows.claim: Commentators support this interpretation by citing God's anger against Jews in 5:60 and the description of people who strayed in 5:77; Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and Mujāhid hold it.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: وتصديق هذا حكم الله عز وجل بالغضب على اليهود (¬5) في قوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The identification also fits a rare accusative reading of ghayr as exception, excluding Jews and Christians from those favored; the author notes that this reading is anomalous.
rows.anchor: وهذا التفسير يوافق في ظاهر اللفظ قراءة من قرأ (غير) بالنصب على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the standard reading, the sense is the path of those favored who are neither under wrath nor astray; denying these traits implicitly attributes them to others, supporting implication in discourse.
rows.anchor: وتصحيح هذا التفسير على القراءة المعروفة هو أن (¬5) المعنى: اهدنا صراط المنعم عليهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and the exegetes have already identified who are under wrath and who are astray.
rows.anchor: قد بينه النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وذكره المفسرون (¬4).

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says sabbiḥ isma rabbika and fasabbiḥ bi-isimi rabbik both occur in Arabic with the same meaning.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: "سبح اسم ربك"، و" [فسبح] باسم ربك (¬2)، كل ذلك قد جاء، وهو كلام العرب (¬3).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author distinguishes them: sabbiḥ bi-ismi rabbik glorifies God by mentioning the name that declares His transcendence above what wrongdoers say.
rows.anchor: هذا كلامه، وكأنة جعلهما (¬4) بمعنى واحد، وبينهما فرق؛ لأن معنى "سبح باسم ربك" نزه الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabbiḥ isma rabbik instead means declare the name free of defect, or say Subḥāna rabbī al-aʿlā, as exegetes explain.
rows.anchor: و"سبح اسم ربك" (نزهه من السوء، وقيل: سبحان ربي الأعلى) (¬6)، # وهذا معنى قول المفسرين

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وابن الزبير
rows.claim: Reports from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ibn al-Zubayr say they recited the verse and said Subḥāna rabbī al-aʿlā.
rows.anchor: وقد روى عن علي (¬2)، وابن عباس (¬3)، وابن الزبير (¬4) (¬5) -رضي الله عنهم- أنهم قرؤوا

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Naẓm uses the phrase to argue that name and named referent are one: one glorifies the name of God by glorifying God, since a name itself cannot be the object of glorification if distinct.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب النظم: قد احتج بهذا الفصل من يقول: إن الاسم، والمسمى واحد؛ لأن أحدا لا يقول:

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says God made what He created in the best form; the segment ends mid-comment.
rows.anchor: قوله: {الذي خلق فسوى} قال عطاء: أحسن ما خلق
